title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
desc: Nvidia has no succession plan and a CEO in hot water, so we’ve drafted a shortlist.
content:
Image Credits: ChatGPT for TechCrunch /

AI

Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors

Connie Loizos

7:13 PM PST · November 11, 2026

It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable and, many would argue, dangerously powerful companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour.

Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates:

Lisa Su . The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival, as well as a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office.

Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets it s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason.

Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more

title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
desc:
Article URL: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/united-airlines-bans-ai-agents-booking-flights/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50458900
Points: 430
# Comments: 414
content:
Watch CBS News

United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.

Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.

To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.

United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.

"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.

United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."

"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

I began using Claude Code about a year ago in September 2025. For a
good week, I woke each morning pinching myself to make sure what I'd
witnessed the day previous actually happened. Its handling of all
aspects of the coding process blew my socks off then, and it's an
order of magnitude more capable now.

On the time scale of our species, the digital age has barely just
begun. When I graduated with a computer science degree, the field was
largely at a stage Churchill might call the "end of the beginning."
And yet, just a quarter-century later, no matter where you turn online
you can't escape the faint but persistent chime of the death knell.
It seems a longstanding problem in maths or theoretical computer
science falls to a toaster on the daily. In what Scott Aaronson is
calling The Mathocalypse, OpenAI's latest model took all of three
hours to carpet bomb 8,000 research problems, resulting in 372 likely
hits, some of them career-makers had they been solved by a human.

When we say "digital age" we mean a state of the art in which sealed
up transistors can reproduce the same outputs given the same inputs
with unerring precision. The power to unambiguously differentiate an
on- versus an off-signal -- the binary "digital" -- might seem
trivial, but is 100% the reason why we're so comfortable handing over
the reins to computers.

And up until the advent of stochastic AI, it's this rigid adherence to
instruction that underlies our world view of technology. So when the
first AI scientists touted their "expert systems," we scut programmers
tittered inwardly. Our sanitized, sequential conception of software
could never admit a ruleset so comprehensive as to cover arbitrary,
unbounded behaviors in a real-world system, one like human dialogue
for instance. RMS appeared in a recent video recounting his CSAIL
work on a circuit analyzer in which he, and I'm paraphrasing, "didn't
model the circuit as a system of equations to be solved, but rather
approached it much as a human would" by applying a series of
diagnostics. I know -- he sounds downright foolish, and would have
sounded so even fifteen years ago. But at the time, rules-based
programming was still novel enough to be considered a viable approach
to AI. In particular, the feedback loop and the physical ergonomics
of programming were vastly improving over workflows only recently
migrated from punch cards. When single computers still occupied
entire rooms, running your program often meant walking it a floor down
then waiting for a slot in the queue, an act of barbarism akin to
dropping off your camera roll at the photomat. When RMS was slumming
it at CSAIL, it was considered a major achievement just to have your

Key Takeaways:

Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild.
Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed.

Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation.

Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn.

Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic s true positive rates into question.

We re seven months into Anthropic s flagship Project Glasswing, and it s time for another update on the results. I ve been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality.

As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers. What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign.

That said, we shouldn t overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model s capabilities.

title: What objective is reasoning solving?
desc:
Article URL: https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50445013
Points: 106
# Comments: 47
content:
What objective is reasoning solving?

Reasoning as pathfinding in token space.

Contents Reasoning as pathfinding. Each sample $z$ is an attempt to find a path from the starting context $x$ to a correct answer $y(z)$ in $\Scal_x$. There s an intuitive but simplified picture of reasoning: let a model think for longer, and it ll be more likely to be correct. This aligns well with our human intuition: spend more time and effort on thinking and it s more likely that we ll arrive at a correct answer.

But this picture doesn t seem to explain everything. During RL training, models learn to write longer chains of thought, and they get more accurate as they do. Yet if you take a trained model and force any one chain to run longer, it helps for a while, then stops helping. 1 Sometimes the answer even gets worse , as if it s overthinking. 2 If a chain of thought were truly converging toward some optimum, more steps shouldn t make it worse. So is it really the length of each chain that helps at inference time? Or is it something more subtle?

This post is my attempt to clarify this confusion (mostly for myself) by looking at reasoning as pathfinding through token space. We ll see that RL maximizes the probability of finding a path from $x$ to $\Scal_x$, but individual paths are not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. As a bonus, this perspective clarifies some odd observations about reasoning models, like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking.

Reasoning as pathfinding #

Ask a reasoning model the same math problem ten times and you ll get ten different chains of thought. Rather than thinking of reasoning as one mysterious process heading toward an answer, let s think of it as pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses one of them with each sample.

Consider the problem: what s $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 10$ ? One solution is to add the numbers one at a time: 1, 3, 6, 10, and so on up to 55. Another way is to pair them from the outside in: $1 + 10$, $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ and $5 + 6$ each make 11, and five pairs of 11 make 55. Both of these paths land on the correct answer, 55.

We can think about reasoning as following this general pattern. We are given a starting point, the prompt, which we ll call $x$.
We want to find a path $z$ that starts from $x$ and ends at a correct answer $y$. To tell whether a path lands in the right place, we assume we have a verifier $r(x, y)$ that returns 1 if $y$ is correct and 0 if it isn t.

So given a starting point $x$, we want to find a path of tokens $z$ that lands in the set

$$\Scal_x = \{y : r(x, y) = 1\}.$$ The figure at the top of this post sketches this picture. Each gray line is a sampled path: it starts from the prompt on the left, meanders in token space by sampling $z$, with some of these paths landing in $\Scal_x$.

title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
desc:
Article URL: https://evanxmerz.com/post/ai-usage-generates-a-fragile-codebase/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50438318
Points: 386
# Comments: 410
content:
AI usage generates a fragile codebase

2026-11-07, Evan X. Merz

programming , artificial intelligence , ai , llm , web programming

I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it.

I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers.

Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame.

In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications.

By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop.

Four ways AI makes codebases fragile

Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase.

1. AI writes shallow tests

One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric.

2. AI writes overly complex ccode

AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult

Key Points

CoreWeave’s bond yield has climbed above 16%, highlighting investor concern about financing the AI infrastructure boom.

Default protection costs have risen across AI-linked companies, including Nvidia, Broadcom and Oracle.

Wall Street expects substantial borrowing to fund further AI expansion, making financing costs a key test for the spending boom.

Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty Images

Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we re hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.

That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away.

That isn t happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave . The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave s five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.

We ve had plenty of warnings from the credit space, said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank s global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, so we ll have to see if credit goes any further.

Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia , Broadcom , and Amazon.com .

CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom s CDS is up 49%, while Amazon s has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia s spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.

Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.

The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.

Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she s not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the s

title: Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans
desc: The AI company is expected to set its valuation range this week, the Wall Street Journal reported.
content:
In Brief

Posted:

5:27 PM PST · November 9, 2026

Image Credits: Ruhani Kaur/Bloomberg / Getty Images

Marina Temkin

Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans

Launching a major tech IPO would seem risky right now, shortly after one of Nasdaq’s biggest sell-offs and amid revelations that a CEO central to the AI boom had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But that isn’t deterring Anthropic, which is moving ahead with its listing plans, according to The Wall Street Journal .

Anthropic plans to set a valuation range this week and begin trading on Thursday or Friday of next week, the Journal reported.

Investors will look to Anthropic’s valuation to gauge the strength of the AI boom. Some institutional investors are now pushing for a valuation below the $1.5 trillion target discussed as recently as last week, a figure that was itself considerably below the $2 trillion floated a few months ago, the report said.

Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators

In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" .

Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."

Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic .

Ingestion Pipeline

When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.

Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:

Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.

Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").

Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.

Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.

If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.

How to Reproduce

Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.

Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.

Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).

title: I'm Not Convinced the AI Bubble Exists
desc:
Article URL: https://matteoraso.github.io/im-not-convinced-the-ai-bubble-exists.html#im-not-convinced-the-ai-bubble-exists
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50418975
Points: 20
# Comm
content:
The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth.

Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained

To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far . It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion , bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.

The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a

title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
desc:
Article URL: https://sergeykuhne.com/blog/fighting-ai-brain-fry
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50416363
Points: 155
# Comments: 130
content:
If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one.

You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab s reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM.

Until you can t. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don t know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish.

A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment.

I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue.

Here is how it actually works.

The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there.

An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine.

What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff.

The reading surface is a Claude artifact. One page, rebuilt from git on every cycle, mirroring the whole board plus a review page per ticket. So I don t scroll back through a terminal trying to reconstruct what a change does. I open one link, read what was built and why, and give my verdict. The verdict goes back into git, onto the card. The page is only a viewer — git is the record.

Then comes the part that matters most.

I take one item. I load its context. I make a decision or request an action. And I close it, by putting it back into the queue.

That closing is the whole trick. The ticket doesn t keep hanging in my memory as a thing to remember about. The context closes with it. So when I pick the next item from the queue, I can actually focus. One thing at a time.

It is still exhausting. But I don t feel distracted or lost.

The challenge was, and still is, the tooling around it. Getting the context served up in a digestible manner, so loading a ticket takes a minute and not twenty. And keeping tickets from going into endless loops because they are blocked waiting for a ruling only I can give.

It s a living organism and I keep improving it. But it felt like a huge step forward in my productivity wi

In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research . The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR.

In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely top down or bottom up , but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion.

We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines.

In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI . On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex- Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. On this page

We changed requirements in a coding benchmark and found models talking themselves out of following them.

Sometimes the agent understood the new requirement perfectly. It described what needed to change, considered an implementation, and then decided the hidden tests probably wanted something else. In one run, a model implemented the change correctly, asked another model for the benchmark’s original answer, and removed its own correct code after receiving it.

This is an awkward habit for a coding assistant to have. It is also a habit that a familiar benchmark can reward. If the model has guessed what the tests expect, it gets the same passing result as an agent that worked carefully from the requirements.

We built MaxxBench to examine how much coding performance depends on those expectations. It changes the instructions or starting code of 89 DeepSWE tasks, giving models familiar engineering work with a reason to revise their usual approach.

Methodology: Small mutations...

Once a benchmark becomes popular, it becomes part of the development process. Its tasks can enter training data. Its scores influence checkpoint selection. Developers adjust prompts and agents against its failures. There are plenty of opportunities to get better at that particular exam. We call gains tied to its particular tasks and conventions benchmaxxing .

Then the scores cluster near the top, and the usual response is a harder benchmark. Recent releases such as FrontierSWE v2 have pushed toward engineering projects that can occupy an agent for much of a day.

We chose DeepSWE’s medium-duration feature-implementation tasks because they are closer to the everyday coding work we wanted to evaluate. Before adding more work, we wanted to know how well models would handle changes to the tasks they already scored well on.

For example, one DeepSWE task asks an agent to write a separate test report for each browser. We added a requirement that the filenames be lowercase. The reporting feature still needs to work; Chrome.xml should now be chrome.xml .

Another task adds retirement dates to FastAPI routes. We changed the required timestamps to UTC with a trailing Z , instead of preserving the supplied time-zone offset.

Anatomy of Apple s Personal Knowledge Graph

Every Mac since macOS 13 (2022) ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph.

The position

A family fork: one knight on e2 attacks White's king, queen, rook and bishop at once. White's pieces are the household the graph is about; the knight is the store, one move from every one of them. White's own last move, 18.e3 , emptied the square it stands on. White is in check and has one legal reply, Kh1 ; then the knight takes the queen. The check falls on the one who accepted the terms. Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo

A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.

The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo , which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.

A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.

The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google

Marina Temkin

5:40 PM PST · November 6, 2026

Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion , confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.

Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.

Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.

Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, bu it announced  plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.

The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.

Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.

The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.

Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion , five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.

Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members , including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.

Security: Follow-up tool call silently routed to a different connector

ChatGPT Apps SDK

AldiPower

November 5, 2026, 9:30am

1

In a conversation with two connectors enabled, ChatGPT made a follow-up tool call through a different connector than the one that started the flow. The user was not told about the switch. The call carried a one-time confirmation code from the first connector’s widget.

Setup

- One ChatGPT account with two connectors enabled that point to the same MCP server.

- Connector A is a custom connector added in developer mode.

- Connector B is the published app from the app directory.

- Each connector has its own OAuth client, so the server sees two separate clients for the same user.

Steps

1. In a conversation with both connectors enabled, ask for an action that needs the user’s confirmation.

2. The model calls a confirmation tool through connector A. Its MCP Apps widget shows the change. The user confirms, and the widget sends a one-time confirmation code to the conversation via ui/message.

3. The model makes the follow-up call with that code, but silently through connector B instead of connector A.

Result

The server rejects the call, because the code is bound to connector A’s OAuth client. Every attempt in that conversation failed. In the attempt we logged in detail, the code was confirmed through connector A and redeemed through connector B. Nothing told the user that the follow-up call went to another connector.

Why this is a problem?

The user starts the flow with connector A and confirms in connector A’s widget. The follow-up call then goes to connector B without the user knowing, and it carries a value produced in connector A’s widget. Connectors are separate apps with separate OAuth grants, so this silent switch passes data from one app to another without the user’s consent.

Here both connectors came from the same provider, so our server-side binding stopped the call. With a third-party connector enabled in the same conversation, we expect the same silent switch to pass one app’s data to another provider if the server URL is shared.

A shared MCP URL is not enough to treat two connectors as one. Behind the same URL, a server can act for different parties depending on the OAuth client, for example separate tenants, partners or environments. The boundary is the connector with its own OAuth client, not the URL.

Expected behavior

Tool calls are matched to a connector by its OAuth client, not by the MCP server URL. A follow-up call goes through the same connector and OAuth client that started the flow.

This post discusses a public METR report on AI R D acceleration at Anthropic. I did not work on this project or see the unredacted report. 1 All opinions are my own and do not represent METR or the report authors.

Thanks to Ryan Greenblatt for discussion, feedback, and help with modeling, and Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, and Hjalmar Wjik for comments.

Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when:

They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R D. 2

This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. 3

For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. 4

The report authors found that:

Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative.

While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.

This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team ) have projected.

Researchers must be sped up a whole lot

Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.

Tencent today announced the release of Tencent Hy4, its latest-generation large language model, marking a significant leap in performance and capabilities that now ranks it among the world s leading open-source AI models. The new model also introduces visual understanding capabilities for the first time, alongside major improvements in instruction following, long-context comprehension and long-horizon agentic tasks, delivering stronger overall performance across a diverse set of applications.

Through advanced visual understanding, reasoning, and tool-calling capabilities, Hy4 now supports a broader range of tasks, including fine-grained image processing, complex chart analysis, and mathematical visual reasoning.

Additionally, Hy4 introduces computer-use capabilities for the first time, enabling it to interact with both command-line interfaces and graphical user interfaces to perform a wide range of work and everyday tasks. The model has undergone specialized training on professional software such as Blender and CAD, significantly enhancing its ability to plan and execute long-horizon and sophisticated tasks.

Deep Model-Product Co-Design Unlocks New Opportunities for Real-World Productivity

Office Productivity Collaboration : Hy4 has significantly enhanced the user experience on Tencent WorkBuddy. Evaluation benchmarks on WorkBuddy show an average performance score of 83.18 and a pass rate of 96.15 percent, with Hy4 ranking first place in nine out of twelve scenarios within the mainland Chinese market. In practical use, Hy4 balances efficiency and effectiveness for visual creative tasks, 3D scene construction, and web development. Apple is reportedly cutting budgets for its internal AI usage

Apple is cutting the daily amount its engineering teams can spend on AI, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. It s a big change for a company that has worked to integrate the technology into its engineering processes.

In October, Apple lowered the daily AI spending cap for its engineering teams, decreasing it from $300 to $200, the outlet reported. And more cuts are in the works, with some allowances falling to $100 a day, sources tell Bloomberg. Outside engineering, Apple is reportedly weighing a daily limit as low as $25 a day.

TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for comment.

Earlier this year, a tsunami of tokenmaxxing took hold, with companies pushing staff to use AI as much as possible in the name of vaguely defined efficiency gains. The frenzy was short-lived, however, as bills for said tokens came due, and companies decided that token rationing might be a more fiscally sensible approach.

Concerns persist about an apparent gap between what AI costs to build and run and the (often unclear) productivity gains the technology is suppose to generate.

Abstract: This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

content:
How I use AI (Oct 2026)

Wow, things have changed.

Last October , I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.

Background

I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/​month in tokens.

In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:

Coding

Research search

Summarization transcription (new) voice

Writing

Art music (new) video

Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy ; we’ll start there.

As before, this remains purely my opinion speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!

My AI policy

This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy ), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.

AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost.

BrainPOP using AI art, perhaps unknowingly

Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.

Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.

Coding

Writing code is solved.

Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code.

Autocomplete is still good (the dim lines)

Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete.

My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create review PRs.

Claude Code adds noise-reduction to (a worktree of) my Mumble client with one prompt

They are nothing short of magic:

They let me build fast : agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio

title: There is no posttraining data commons
desc:
Article URL: https://openathena.ai/blog/there-is-no-posttraining-data-commons/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50352641
Points: 33
# Comments: 7
content:
There is no posttraining data commons

October 15, 2026
·
David Hall

·

EXPLAINER

We got extraordinarily lucky with pretraining data. Training large language models required a truly vast corpus of text, and it was just kind of lying around.

Not exactly by accident. For the last 50 or so years, humanity has been busily creating and digitizing an enormous public record of human knowledge. Most obviously, Wikipedia’s editors have assembled the most comprehensive encyclopedia humanity has ever produced. A vigorous open source movement created a couple petabytes of software source code. Communities on Stack Exchange spent more than a decade asking questions, arguing about answers, and carefully curating the results. Scientists uploaded their papers to ArXiv. Project Gutenberg—almost as old as the internet itself—produced digital editions of out-of-copyright books.

And of course, billions of people made websites, commented, had arguments both petty and profound, uploaded photos and paintings, wrote fiction, and—believe it or not—sometimes went and told lies on the internet.

Efforts like Gutenberg, Internet Archive, Wikipedia, ArXiv, and Stack Exchange were self-conscious efforts at creating a digital knowledge commons. And then there’s Common Crawl. Since 2007, Common Crawl has been regularly archiving snapshots of a sizable subset of the internet, and then making it freely available for anyone to access and use. Today, there’s something like 10 petabytes of data archived by Common Crawl.

This vast commons of human knowledge formed the basis for the LLM revolution. GPT-3 was trained on about 60% Common Crawl-derived data. The original Llama data mix was almost entirely extracted from the internet commons. 1

That’s not to say that refining the raw material of the web into LLM-ready chunks was simple. Web pages are extraordinarily messy creatures, and a large fraction of the web is spam or junk intended to fool Google’s crawler. People are still writing papers on how to do filtering, HTML-to-text extraction, old document OCR, and synthetic rewriting.

Though the incumbent large players have seemingly moved on with their own custom web crawlers ( Cloudflare reports that over half of crawler traffic is for AI ), modern open LLMs like Nemotron and our own still rely on this commons for the vast majority of their pretraining data. Without continued access to this commons, truly open LLMs cannot exist.

These days, the focus of frontier AI research has shifted to posttraining, particularly so-called “agentic” AI. Like pretraining before it, posttraining requires vast amounts of compute and vast amounts of data. However, there isn’t the same ready-made trove of raw data lying around for posttraining. In short, there is no posttraining data commons.

The fundamental difference is simple: Pretraining consumes documents, while posttraining consumes tasks. 2 But “task” here is already an abstraction. The tasks used by reinforcement learning for posttraining

Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses

Jagmeet Singh

7:30 PM PST · November 2, 2026

Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users digital activity to a broader audience.

On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.

Introduced in June, Google s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.

Google said it chose India as Dreambeans first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.

Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.

In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.

Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing.

That could limit Dreambeans appeal in India, where many people regularly switch

Lucas Ropek

Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth .

However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear.

When discussing how AI could potentially contribute to revenue growth over time, Kevan Parekh, Apple s chief financial officer, said: On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.

Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.

Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business.

During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company s service business could expand into new territory.

Y Combinator s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens

Julie Bort

4:35 PM PST · November 2, 2026

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he s suffered from cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast  The Builders , set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.

I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens, he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack , on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.

On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.

It s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years, he said.

He describes using AI agents as getting help with almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, What about this? Or it ll help you see around corners.

As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human, he said.

For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is rebuilding the way we operate at YC, he said. We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we ve ever backed, anyone who s ever emailed us, like all the applications.

Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.

It s too expensive right now, he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.

title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
desc:
Article URL: https://www.techpolicy.press/the-sec-should-block-anthropics-ipo-to-protect-the-public/

content:
Perspective

The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public

Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026 Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts .

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Republish

Share

Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.

That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.

The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.

Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.

Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.

The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.

Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.

Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land

AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says

AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).

Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S P 493 — the S P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.

“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.

Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”

“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”

Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains .

title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
desc:
Article URL: https://nolanlawson.com/2026/10/28/the-ai-cost-of-javascript-frameworks/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50323088
Points: 296
# Comments: 228
content:
Skip to content One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway).

For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.)

But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?”

Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward:

Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised)

Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.)

Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating)

Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse

The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.:

I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test.

To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR ), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else?

Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too .

The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “ the issue” in the presidential election.

So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits” ; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.”

Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments ) as “good and healthy.”

“Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI.

In Mayer’s case, that involved asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter . For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school and also declaring that he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT . Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to meet your social and romantic needs through AI .

This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people — a crucial question with Anthropic set to go public just as Wall Street begins losing its appetite for heavy AI spending .

On the latest episode of the Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem.

Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.”

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.

AI text watermarking and quality loss

Aug 24, 2026

4

1

1

Share

After the EU AI Act’s transparency guidelines went into effect, and following the announcement that most major AI labs will soon be watermarking their text output to comply, there has been some debate about how much of an impact this is going to have, if any, on the quality of the text produced by AI models.

Since the focus of AI labs shifted to code production, I think the written output of the models has gotten much worse. 1 But it’s still interesting to try to understand if watermarking could make it even worse.

I found the discussion around technology writer John Gruber’s recent post, Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing , very interesting.

On watermarking, Gruber wrote:

It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance.

He got a lot of pushback, with many debating how you would even measure quality, or define it.

But some argued that watermarking does not affect quality at all: it’s essentially just using different random numbers to generate the text. Daniel Jalkut, whom Gruber linked to in his follow-up, published a piece titled AI Can’t Adulterate its Own Writing , in which he wrote:

…there are also ways of tweaking the algorithm that would not diminish its randomness. For example if a random number generator routinely reversed the order of the digits in a generated number, the randomness would remain the same.

Similarly, in another discussion, someone described it as essentially swapping two faces of a die.

In a follow-up piece , Gruber wrote:

I hope that’s true. I believe it’s possible that it is true. I think it’s highly unlikely that it is true.

I think Gruber is right.

Quality loss across responses

Anthropic make a bold claim: “ Watermarking does not impact the quality of Claude’s output. ” The paper they link to and based their design on (Google’s SynthID-Text, published in Nature in 2024) assures everyone that the method “ preserves response quality ”.

So it’s easy to assume there’s been a lot of fuss over nothing, that they really are just swapping some random numbers around.

But their no-quality-impact claim, which they tested with humans, is based on single responses. Not the way millions of people actually use these systems: as back-and-forth conversations, over time, over multiple prompts and responses.

The 56-page supplementary PDF they link to at the bottom provides some more info on the method used, and it suggests the no-quality-impact claim isn’t telling the full story. Notably, it says that there is a “diversity/detectability trade-off”:

While single-sequence non-distortion guarantees the quality of each individual response, it does not necessarily preserve diversity across multiple responses

bootgpt

A neural network that boots your PC.

The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model
from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS,
no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log:
timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.

Build thread: https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757

With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality
you get:

[ 2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine
[ 1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg
[ 0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ...
[ 1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212
[ 1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16

Run it

brew install nasm qemu
python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install numpy
./build.sh
./run.sh

disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS
box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.

Pieces

corpus_gen.py makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk
per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that
repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.

train.py trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax)
and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot
sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The
script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG
sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be
diffed. They match char for char.

boot.asm is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to
print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with
timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.

record.py records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor
socket. No window involved.

The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all
live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS
plumbing into 510 bytes.

title: Do the math: How we took over ChatGPT accounts
desc:

content:
Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

By bypassing ChatGPT s sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone s account simply by sending them a link.

Mukul Goyal Oct 28, 2026 12 mins

October 26, 2026 Fixed

P1 Severity

In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.

The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.

The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.

flowchart TD
A[ Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation ] -- B[ Victim opens the public share ]

It started with a graph and a Preview

The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.
